title: Pattern Sequencer
blurb: Record your pads into a pattern, fix it step by step, and chain patterns into an arrangement.

steps.title: Choose a pattern slot and tempo
body: Press PATTERN SELECT and pick an empty pattern slot to work in.
Set the tempo and pattern length before recording — changing length later can truncate what you played.
Turn the metronome on so your take has something to lock to.
steps.checkpoint: An empty pattern is selected and the click is running at your chosen tempo.
steps.tip: Two bars is the right length for a first pattern. You can always chain two patterns rather than recording one long one.

steps.title: Record in real time
body: Press REC to arm the pattern, then play your pads in time with the click.
The sequencer captures your timing and velocity as you play, so play it like a performance rather than a data entry task.
Let it loop and keep playing — you can add layers on each pass.
steps.checkpoint: The pattern plays your part back without you touching the pads.
steps.tip: Record one voice per pass — kick first, then snare, then hats. Layering is far more accurate than trying to play everything at once.

steps.title: Step-record with TR-REC
body: For patterns that need to be exact, use TR-REC instead of playing live.
Select the pad you want to program, then switch on the steps where it should trigger.
This is the fastest way to build machine-tight hi-hats or a four-on-the-floor kick.
Move to the next pad and repeat until the pattern is complete.
steps.checkpoint: Steps you enabled trigger exactly on the grid, dead on time.
steps.tip: Mix both methods: step-record the drums so they are rigid, then play the melodic pads in live so they breathe.

steps.title: Fix and refine
body: Play the pattern back and listen for the one thing that bothers you most, rather than trying to fix everything at once.
Clear a pad's part and re-record just that voice if a layer is off.
Adjust velocities so accents stand out — a pattern with flat dynamics sounds programmed, not played.
steps.checkpoint: The loop is something you would happily hear repeat twenty times.
steps.tip: If a part never sits right, the problem is usually the sample's start point, not your timing. Go back and re-trim it.

steps.title: Chain patterns into an arrangement
body: Record a second pattern as a variation — drop the hats, change the kick, add a fill.
Chain the patterns in the order you want them to play so a loop becomes a track with sections.
Then resample the whole chain to a pad if you want to build further on top of it.
steps.checkpoint: Patterns play back in sequence without you switching them by hand.
steps.tip: Small variation goes a long way: one pattern with hats and one without is enough to imply an arrangement.
